name: Stimulus die
intent: Inject a random prompt to break fixation and force a new angle.
when: the obvious options are exhausted and thinking has gone in circles

variants.label: Cut, fold and tape a die
Roll any die against a printed table
variants.prompt: No cutting: roll any six-sided die, or use the last digit of the clock's seconds, and look up the matching row on the printed table. Answer whatever it lands on.
variants.readback: Random outputs are prompts, not answers; read the human's response to the row, not the row itself.

prompt: Cut out the die, fold it, roll it when you are stuck, and answer whatever it lands on.
readback: Random outputs are prompts, not answers; read the human's response to the face, not the face.

claims.claim: Exposure to randomly selected stimuli (words or prompts unrelated to the problem) during idea generation increases the number and originality of ideas, compared with generating without stimuli.
claims.construct: random entry / external stimulation in idea generation

claims.claim: Prompting idea generation with generic transformation heuristics ("reverse it", "make it 10×", "borrow from another field") increases the variety and creativity of generated concepts, compared with unprompted generation.
claims.construct: design heuristics / transformation operators; analogical transfer

claims.claim: Impasses in problem solving are overcome when the solver relaxes a self-imposed constraint on the solution, so deliberately removing a constraint makes new solution paths available.

grounding.helps: when the same few ideas keep recurring during a divergent phase; heuristic prompts reduced fixation in one design study, and rolling operators at random is otherwise untested
grounding.backfires: when the face rolled does not fit the problem, when the prompt itself becomes the fixation, and during convergence or evaluation, where random input is noise
